tytul: Daniel 2. The Dream of the Statue
opis: A dream no one could tell. A God who reveals mysteries, and a kingdom without end.
zdanie: Empires come and go, and history still ends with a stone that no human hand cut out.

elementy.tekst: This chapter most often turns into a history lesson with a chart: metal, empire, dates. This meeting takes a different path. It asks what kind of God reveals mysteries, and what this dream gave to people who had lost their country, their king, and their temple. The wise men of Babylon say the gods do not dwell among mortals. Daniel says there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries. The whole chapter stretches between those two sentences.
The chapter is long. At level 1 you read five sections, and what lies between them is summarized in one sentence in italics. Read it aloud to the group.
**Where the landmines are:**

pozycje: Someone may know the prophetic interpretation by heart and want to deliver it right away, with dates. Ask them to wait until block 5, and stick to what is in the text. The text names only the first kingdom.

A conversation about kingdoms easily drifts into current politics, the European Union, wars, and leaders. Don’t go there. This material doesn’t point to any modern state or politician, and neither should the group.
Someone at the table may have heard about prophecy only in a tone meant to frighten. This dream doesn’t frighten. It ends with good news.
Someone may ask whether the book was written after the events it describes. That is a serious question, and it is discussed at level 3.

elementy.tekst: **What not to do:** don’t draw a chart before the group has described the statue for themselves. Don’t add dates that aren’t in the text. Don’t settle disputes between schools of interpretation in a tone that shuts the conversation down.
Think of a time when someone demanded something impossible from you. Say in one sentence what you did first.
answer first, and keep it short. Don’t comment on other people’s answers.

akapity: In the second year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar had dreams that troubled his spirit, and sleep escaped him. So the king gave orders to summon the magicians, enchanters, sorcerers, and astrologers to explain his dreams. When they came and stood before the king, he said to them, “I have had a dream, and my spirit is anxious to understand it.”

elementy.tekst: The wise men ask the king to tell them the dream, and they will interpret it. The king refuses: they must tell him both the dream and its interpretation, or they will die. He suspects they are stalling for time.

akapity: The astrologers answered the king, “No one on earth can do what the king requests! No king, however great and powerful, has ever asked anything like this of any magician, enchanter, or astrologer. What the king requests is so difficult that no one can tell it to him except the gods, whose dwelling is not with mortals.” This response made the king so furious with anger that he gave orders to destroy all the wise men of Babylon.

elementy.tekst: The king demands not only the interpretation but the dream itself. **What is he afraid of? Whom does he not trust?**
The empire’s best experts say the gods’ “dwelling is not with mortals.” **What does that one sentence say about the whole religion they represent?** What is it like to live with gods like that?
The most powerful man in the world can’t sleep and passes a death sentence on his own advisers. **What does power look like when it is afraid?**

In the ancient Near East a king’s dream was not his private business. It was considered a message from the gods, often a warning of disaster threatening the ruler or the state. The king had to know its meaning so he could protect himself in time. Nebuchadnezzar behaves like a man who has received an urgent dispatch and can’t decode it. He is at the beginning of his reign and isn’t sure of anything yet.

bloki.tytul: Context: Where We Are in the Book

elementy.tekst: **Where we are.** In the second of the six court stories. Chapter 1 showed how Daniel came to Babylon and completed the royal school. Now he is the youngest of the wise men, and no one has even called him to the council. This chapter is the axis of the whole book: the dream of four kingdoms and the kingdom of God will return in chapter 7 as Daniel’s own vision, and chapters 8-12 will develop it.

**Background.** In verse 4 the text notes that the wise men answer in Aramaic. From that point to the end of chapter 7, the book itself is written in Aramaic, the official language of the empire. The part about the destiny of the nations is written so that the nations could read it.
The first verse says “in the second year.” That matters for the story: in Nebuchadnezzar’s second year, Daniel is still very young, at most just out of the royal school.
**What does it change in this scene to know that the one about to stand before the king is not an experienced dignitary, but someone at the very start of his career?**

akapity: So the decree went out that the wise men were to be executed, and men went to look for Daniel and his friends to execute them. When Arioch, the commander of the king’s guard, had gone out to execute the wise men of Babylon, Daniel replied with discretion and tact. “Why is the decree from the king so harsh?” he asked. At this time Arioch explained the situation to Daniel. So Daniel went in and asked the king to give him some time, so that he could give him the interpretation. Then Daniel returned to his house and explained the matter to his friends Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, urging them to plead for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that Daniel and his friends would not be killed with the rest of the wise men of Babylon. During the night, the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision, and he blessed the God of heaven

elementy.tekst: Daniel finds out he is to die for something he hasn’t even heard about. **List, in order, what he does in verses 14-18.** What is missing from that list that you might have expected?
He asks the king for time and his friends for prayer. He promises an interpretation before he knows anything. **Where does that confidence come from, and why, even so, doesn’t he pray alone?**
They pray for “mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery.” **Besides themselves, for whom else are they standing up in this prayer?** Look at the end of verse 18.

bloki.tytul: There Is a God in Heaven

akapity: and declared: “Blessed be the name of God forever and ever, for wisdom and power belong to Him. He changes the times and seasons; He removes kings and establishes them. He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to the discerning. He reveals the deep and hidden things; He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him. To You, O God of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, because You have given me wisdom and power. And now You have made known to me what we have requested, for You have made known to us the dream of the king.”

elementy.tekst: Daniel goes to Arioch and asks him to stop the executions. Arioch hurries him to the king. The king asks: can you really tell me the dream and interpret it?

akapity: Daniel answered the king, “No wise man, enchanter, medium, or magician can explain to the king the mystery of which he inquires. But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and He has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the latter days. Your dream and the visions that came into your mind as you lay on your bed were these: As you lay on your bed, O king, your thoughts turned to the future, and the Revealer of Mysteries made known to you what will happen. And to me this mystery has been revealed, not because I have more wisdom than any man alive, but in order that the interpretation might be made known to the king, and that you may understand the thoughts of your mind.

elementy.tekst: Daniel has the answer, and the executioner is still going through the city. **What does he do first?** What does that order say about him?
“He removes kings and establishes them.” **How does that sentence sound from a man whose own king has just been removed, and who now serves the one who did it?**
Compare verse 11 with verse 28. **What does Daniel say about himself, and what about God?** According to verse 30, whom is the dream for?

The wise men told the truth about their gods: they don’t dwell among people and they don’t speak. Daniel answers with one sentence: there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries. He doesn’t hide them; He discloses them, and to whom? To a pagan king who destroyed His city. The first thing Nebuchadnezzar learns about Daniel’s God is that this God wants to talk with him.

akapity: Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I had a dream, and no one can interpret it. But I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream you can interpret it.” “I myself cannot do it,” Joseph replied, “but God will give Pharaoh a sound answer.”

elementy.tekst: A young Hebrew, a foreign court, a ruler’s dream, helpless wise men. **What connects Joseph’s answer with Daniel’s?** What are both of them careful about at a moment that could have been their big chance?
**Why is it so hard to say “I myself cannot do it” when everyone is watching and waiting for a performance?**

akapity: As you, O king, were watching, a great statue appeared. A great and dazzling statue stood before you, and its form was awesome. The head of the statue was pure gold, its chest and arms were silver, its belly and thighs were bronze, its legs were iron, and its feet were part iron and part clay. As you watched, a stone was cut out, but not by human hands. It struck the statue on its feet of iron and clay, and crushed them. Then the iron, clay, bronze, silver, and gold were shattered and became like chaff on the threshing floor in summer. The wind carried them away, and not a trace of them could be found. But the stone that had struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.

elementy.tekst: **Describe the statue from top to bottom, using only the text.** What changes as your eyes move downward?
Now the stone. **Where does it come from, by whose hand, and what happens to it at the end?** Set the statue and the stone side by side: what in this dream is made by human hands, and what isn’t?
All that is left of the statue is “chaff on the threshing floor,” carried away by the wind. **What does that picture say about things that look eternal?**

From the head downward, the metals lose value and gain hardness: gold, silver, bronze, iron. The pattern breaks at the feet, where iron is mixed with clay. So the statue is weakest exactly where it ought to be strongest, because everything stands on the feet. The stone doesn’t strike the golden head. It strikes the feet.

akapity: This was the dream; now we will tell the king its interpretation. You, O king, are the king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given sovereignty, power, strength, and glory. Wherever the sons of men or beasts of the field or birds of the air dwell, He has given them into your hand and has made you ruler over them all. You are that head of gold. But after you, there will arise another kingdom, inferior to yours. Next, a third kingdom, one of bronze, will rule the whole earth. Finally, there will be a fourth kingdom as strong as iron; for iron shatters and crushes all things, and like iron that crushes all things, it will shatter and crush all the others. And just as you saw that the feet and toes were made partly of fired clay and partly of iron, so this will be a divided kingdom, yet some of the strength of iron will be in it—just as you saw the iron mixed with clay. And as the toes of the feet were partly iron and partly clay, so this kingdom will be partly strong and partly brittle. As you saw the iron mixed with clay, so the peoples will mix with one another, but will not hold together any more than iron mixes with clay. In the days of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people. It will shatter all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, but will itself stand forever. And just as you saw a stone being cut out of the mountain without human hands, and it shattered the iron, bronze, clay, silver, and gold, so the great God has told the king what will happen in the future. The dream is true, and its interpretation is trustworthy.”

elementy.tekst: Nebuchadnezzar hears, almost in one breath: “You are that head of gold” and “after you, there will arise another kingdom.” **What is it like to hear both at once?** According to verse 37, where did the king get what he has?
**From verse 44, list everything the text says about God’s kingdom.** How is it different from the four before it?

The first readers of this book lived under foreign rule, without a king and without a temple. **What did this dream give them?** What difference does it make in everyday life to know that history has a final chapter and that no empire will write it?
Iron and clay: “the peoples will mix with one another, but will not hold together.” **What does that say about all attempts to glue the world together by human means?**

the text names only the first kingdom, Babylon. If the group starts naming the next ones, ask: “Where does it say that in this chapter?” The book itself gives the names of the following kingdoms, but later on. They are at level 2.

bloki.tytul: The Book Names the Next Ones Itself

akapity: Now this is the inscription that was written: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN. And this is the interpretation of the message: MENE means that God has numbered the days of your reign and brought it to an end. TEKEL means that you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient. PERES means that your kingdom has been divided and given over to the Medes and Persians.”
The two-horned ram that you saw represents the kings of Media and Persia. The shaggy goat represents the king of Greece, and the large horn between his eyes is the first king.

elementy.tekst: The book of Daniel itself gives the names of the second and third kingdoms. **Which kingdoms are they?** What follows from that for the fourth, which comes after Greece and is “as strong as iron”?
**Why is it better for the Bible itself to explain its symbols than for us to match them to whatever we happen to see in the news?**

Daniel never names the fourth kingdom. Already in ancient times many readers, Jewish and Christian, saw it as Rome, which came after Greece and was not replaced by any further empire, only by a patchwork of states, strong and brittle, never lastingly joined together. This is also how the Seventh-day Adventist Church reads this dream. But it is worth keeping the proportions in mind: the text spends nine verses on the kingdoms in order to arrive at the tenth.

akapity: He put before them another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that a man planted in his field. Although it is the smallest of all seeds, yet it grows into the largest of garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches.”

elementy.tekst: Jesus’ listeners knew Daniel’s dream and were waiting for the stone that would crush Rome. Jesus tells them about a seed. **What do these two pictures of the kingdom have in common, and how are they different?**
**Do the stone and the seed rule each other out, or do they describe two stages of the same story?** What would that mean for people who live in between?

akapity: At this, King Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face, paid homage to Daniel, and ordered that an offering of incense be presented to him. The king said to Daniel, “Your God is truly the God of gods and Lord of kings, the Revealer of Mysteries, since you were able to reveal this mystery.” Then the king promoted Daniel and gave him many generous gifts. He made him ruler over the entire province of Babylon and chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon. And at Daniel’s request, the king appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to manage the province of Babylon, while Daniel remained in the king’s court.

elementy.tekst: The king says great things about God. **But look closely at the pronoun: whose God is He, according to the king?** What is still missing from his response?

bloki.tytul: The Word: Authority Borrowed from Eden

elementy.tekst: Verse 38 describes Nebuchadnezzar’s authority over people, the beasts of the field, and the birds of the air. It sounds like an echo of the first page of the Bible.

akapity: God blessed them and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it; rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air and every creature that crawls upon the earth.”

elementy.tekst: **What is on Nebuchadnezzar’s list that wasn’t on Adam and Eve’s?** What does it say about empires that in the beginning humans were given authority over creation, but not over other humans?

Daniel tells the king that the God of heaven “has given” him all this. It is the same verb that came up three times in chapter 1. **What does it mean for a ruler, and for each of us, that what we have is given and not won?**

bloki.tytul: Tension: How This Dream Has Been Read

elementy.tekst: This chapter has been read in several ways, and it is only honest to name them.

The historicist school is the oldest. It holds that Daniel wrote the book in the sixth century BC and that the dream covers the whole course of history: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome, a divided Europe, and at the end the kingdom of God at Christ’s second coming. This is how the Reformers read it, and how Adventists read it. The futurist school agrees about the author and the kingdoms, but moves the final part of Daniel’s prophecies entirely into a short period just before the end of the world. The preterist school holds that everything was fulfilled in ancient times, at the latest with Jesus’ first coming or the fall of Rome. The historical-critical school holds that the book was written by an unknown author in the second century BC, after most of the events it describes, and therefore makes Greece the fourth kingdom and splits the Medes and the Persians into two separate kingdoms.

Two things are worth knowing here. The book itself treats the Medes and Persians as one kingdom, as can be seen in Daniel 5:28 and 8:20. And among the Dead Sea Scrolls there are manuscripts of Daniel from the second century BC, which means the book was already being copied and read as Scripture at that time.

A separate question concerns the stone. Some see it as Jesus’ first coming and the slow growth of the church. Others point out that the stone strikes the feet, that is, it comes after the fourth kingdom has been divided; that its impact is a catastrophe for the whole statue, not a quiet beginning; and that in the dream the stone’s kingdom doesn’t exist alongside the earlier ones but takes their place. That points to the second coming. Jesus Himself took up this image:

akapity: But Jesus looked directly at them and said, “Then what is the meaning of that which is written: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’? Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed.”

elementy.tekst: Jesus speaks of a stone one can fall on now and a stone that will fall later. **How does this saying help bring the two readings together?**
All the schools differ over dates and names. **What do they agree on when they read verse 44?** What remains of this chapter even if someone isn’t sure of the details?
you don’t have to defend any school. It is enough to show that the historicist reading holds to the names the book itself gives. If someone has a different view, ask which verse they base it on.
Everyone has their own statue: something that looks as lasting as gold, on which they rest their sense of security. **What is it for you, and where are its feet of clay?**
In a crisis Daniel asked for time and for the prayers of three friends. **Whom can you ask when you are given a task beyond your strength?** What holds you back?
If you want to share: **is there something in your life you don’t understand, which you carry around like the king with his unexplained dream?** You don’t have to say what it is.

bloki.tytul: A Question Without an Easy Answer

elementy.tekst: Daniel says that God “removes kings and establishes them,” and that it was God who gave the kingdom to Nebuchadnezzar, the very man who burned Jerusalem. **Does that mean God wants whatever government happens to be in power? How do we reconcile a God who holds history in His hands with a history full of wrongs done by rulers?**

don’t close this question, and don’t let it turn into a conversation about today’s politicians. It is worth letting one observation from the text itself be made: the dream praises none of the four kingdoms. They all end up as chaff. God permits and limits, and that is not the same as approving.
Empires come and go, and history still ends with a stone that no human hand cut out.
**Memory verse:** Daniel 2:44 or Daniel 2:28a.

The wise men of Babylon believed in gods who don’t dwell among people and don’t speak. Ask yourself honestly: **in everyday life, is my God closer to Daniel’s God or to the gods of Babylon?** Do I expect Him to say anything to me?

Think of the thing whose collapse you fear most: your job, your health, your savings, the world order you know. Tell God exactly what you are afraid of. Then read Daniel 2:44 aloud and stay with that sentence a little longer than is comfortable.
**For the brave:** this week, ask a specific person to pray with you about something you have been carrying alone until now.

**Someone launches straight into the whole interpretation: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome, Europe, with dates.** Thank them and ask for patience: “We’ll get to that in block 5. First let’s see what comes before the statue.” If the lecture comes back, ask every time: “Where does it say that in the text in front of us?”

**“This is happening right now, look at what the European Union is doing,” or some other current topic.** Interrupt calmly. The dream says that no human structure will glue the world together for good, and nothing more. It doesn’t point to institutions or dates. Go back to the question of what this dream gave the exiles and what it gives us.

**“But this book was written after the fact; every historian knows that.”** Don’t get defensive. Say that this view exists and that there are serious reasons to disagree with it, including the manuscripts from Qumran and the fact that the book itself joins the Medes with the Persians. Suggest level 3 or a conversation after the meeting. Don’t turn it into an argument at the table.

**Someone is frightened: “So the world will end, and everything will fall apart.”** Point out who in this chapter is afraid and who is singing. The king, who has everything, is afraid. Daniel, who has nothing, blesses God. The dream doesn’t end in catastrophe but in a kingdom that “will itself stand forever.” For the exiles, that was the best news there could be.
**The conversation gets stuck on details: how many toes, exactly which countries, what the clay means.** The text doesn’t count toes or name countries. Say so plainly and move on to verse 44.

**Someone asks: “Why doesn’t God answer me the way He answered Daniel, in one night?”** This is real pain; don’t brush it off. Don’t promise that an answer will come. You can say that Daniel, too, received only what he asked for that night, and that he waited his whole life for answers to many other questions, as the following chapters will show. Stay with that person after the meeting.
**The group is silent after a question.** Count to ten in your head. If the silence continues, repeat the question in the same words.
**You won’t get through all the material.** Just read block 2 aloud. Don’t shorten block 3, because without it the meeting turns into a history lesson. From block 5, keep the question about verse 44.
